read.sections.0.heading.source: Art that does not last, memory that does
read.sections.0.heading.back: Art that does not last, memory that lasts

read.sections.0.text.source:
An artwork does not have to last for centuries to matter. Flowers, food, paper and short-lived structures can bring people together around a shared memory. In Mexico, Día de Muertos, or Day of the Dead, joins artistic making with remembering people after their death. Its meanings belong to living communities, whose practices keep changing.

UNESCO recognises the festival as practised by Mexico's Indigenous communities. It lists it as intangible heritage: knowledge and practices passed between people. UNESCO's account describes celebrations in late October and early November. This is near the end of the season when maize grows. For people who hold this belief, relatives who have died return for a short time. Families prepare favourite foods. They arrange flowers, candles and paper decorations. These actions keep up bonds between generations. They help people feel part of a community. You can study this belief without sharing it.
read.sections.0.text.back:
An artwork does not have to last for centuries to be important. Flowers, food, paper and buildings that stand only for a short while can gather people around a shared memory. In Mexico, Día de Muertos, or the Day of the Dead, joins the activity of making art with remembering people who have died. Its meanings belong to living communities, whose practices keep changing.

UNESCO recognises this celebration as practised by Mexico's Indigenous peoples. UNESCO records it as intangible cultural heritage: knowledge and practices passed on from person to person. UNESCO's account describes celebrations at the end of October and the beginning of November. This time is close to the end of the maize-growing season. For people who hold this belief, relatives who have died return for a short time. Families prepare their favourite foods. They arrange flowers, candles and paper decorations. These activities keep the bonds between generations. They help people feel part of a community. You can study this belief without sharing it.
read.sections.0.text.note: "Day of the Dead" is "Hari Orang Mati", its usual Indonesian name; elsewhere the lesson says "orang yang sudah meninggal" (people who have passed away), the gentle form. "intangible heritage" is "warisan budaya takbenda", as in Lesson 17.

read.sections.0.simpler.source:
Art does not have to last to matter. Flowers, food and paper can bring people together to remember. In Mexico, Día de Muertos means Day of the Dead. People make art to keep the dead in mind. It belongs to living people, and it keeps changing.

UNESCO says Indigenous groups in Mexico practise it. It calls it intangible heritage. That means skills and ways that people pass on. It comes in late October and early November. That is when the maize, or corn, season ends. Some people believe that relatives who have died come back for a short time. Families cook the foods these relatives liked. They set out flowers, candles and paper. This links old and young. It helps them feel they belong. You can learn about a belief and not share it.
read.sections.0.simpler.back:
Art does not have to last long to be important. Flowers, food and paper can gather people to remember. In Mexico, Día de Muertos means the Day of the Dead. People make art to remember people who have passed away. This celebration belongs to people who are still living, and it keeps changing.

UNESCO says Indigenous peoples in Mexico practise it. UNESCO calls it intangible cultural heritage. That means skills and ways that people pass on. This celebration comes at the end of October and the beginning of November. At that time the maize season ends. Some people believe that relatives who have passed away come back for a short while. Families cook the foods those relatives used to like. They set out flowers, candles and paper. This connects old and young. This helps them feel part of their group. You can study a belief without sharing it.

read.sections.1.heading.source: Histories of change, many local forms
read.sections.1.heading.back: Histories of change, many local forms

read.sections.1.text.source:
These practices have histories of change. In the sixteenth century, Europeans brought Catholic feasts to Mexico. Indigenous religious traditions became linked with them. All Saints' Day falls on 1 November, and All Souls' Day on 2 November. Religious images and older practices could take on meanings together. But not every Indigenous people, Mexican family or Catholic community celebrates in the same way. Place, family traditions and beliefs shape different forms.

For example, in the Huasteca region the festival is called Xantolo. It includes processions, or walking parades, with masked performers called Huehues. UNESCO's account says that costumes, music and characters differ from one community to the next. So a national festival name holds many local histories. A public museum display also has a different setting and audience from an ofrenda in a family home. An ofrenda is an offering. The word also means the arranged altar or display of offerings.
read.sections.1.text.back:
These practices have a history of change. In the 16th century, Europeans brought Catholic feast days to Mexico. The religious traditions of Indigenous peoples became connected with them. All Saints' Day falls on 1 November, and All Souls' Day on 2 November. Religious images and older practices could gain meanings together. But not every Indigenous people, Mexican family or Catholic community celebrates it in the same way. Place, family traditions and beliefs shape different forms.

For example, in the Huasteca region this celebration is called Xantolo. This celebration includes processions, or parades on foot, with masked performers called Huehues. UNESCO's account says that the costumes, music and characters differ from one community to another. So one national celebration name holds many local histories. A display in a public museum also has a different setting and audience from an ofrenda in a family home. An ofrenda is an offering. This word also means the altar or display where offerings are arranged.
read.sections.1.text.note: The feast days use the Indonesian Catholic names ("Hari Raya Semua Orang Kudus", "Peringatan Arwah Semua Orang Beriman"); the simpler text shortens the second to "Hari Arwah". Reviewers: check with a Catholic reader.

read.sections.1.simpler.source:
These ways have changed. In the 1500s, Europeans brought Catholic feast days to Mexico. Old Indigenous ways became linked with them. All Saints' Day is on 1 November, and All Souls' Day on 2 November. Old ways and Catholic images came to share meanings. But not every family or group does the same. Place, family and belief make each one its own.

In the Huasteca region, the festival is called Xantolo. People walk in a line, with masked performers called Huehues. UNESCO says the clothes, music and roles differ from group to group. So one name holds many local stories. An ofrenda is an offering. It is also the altar where offerings are set out. A museum ofrenda is for the public. It differs from one in a home.
read.sections.1.simpler.back:
These practices have changed. In the 1500s, Europeans brought Catholic feast days to Mexico. The old ways of Indigenous peoples became connected with them. All Saints' Day falls on 1 November, and All Souls' Day on 2 November. Old ways and Catholic images began to share meanings. But not every family or group does the same thing. Place, family and belief make each celebration different.

In the Huasteca region, this celebration is called Xantolo. People walk in a line, with masked performers called Huehues. UNESCO says their clothes, music and roles differ from group to group. So one name holds many local stories. An ofrenda is an offering. An ofrenda is also the altar where offerings are arranged. An ofrenda in a museum is made for the public. That ofrenda is different from an ofrenda at home.

read.sections.2.heading.source: Paper, arrangement and a printed skeleton
read.sections.2.heading.back: Paper, arrangement and a skeleton in a print

read.sections.2.text.source:
An ofrenda gives memory a shape people can see. Photographs, food, flowers and other objects can show who is being remembered. They also make the space welcoming. The museum example in the photograph is in Coyoacán, in Mexico City. It has stepped levels, bright paper decoration and model skeleton figures. Its file record says it is dedicated to the Virgin of Guadalupe. This display brings Catholic images and festive making together in one public space. It cannot stand for every household altar.

Papel picado, paper with cut-out designs, needs knowledge of pattern and material. Makers cut designs into thin tissue paper and join the sheets into banners. Skilled artisans can cut several layers at once, repeating a design. The paper may not last long, but the knowledge of making it continues. Setting up a short-lived altar also takes planning, choices and work. The finished photograph shows only part of this.

Printed images have also changed how the festival looks in public. José Guadalupe Posada's Calavera Catrina shows a skeleton wearing a grand hat. A calavera is a skull, or an artistic image of a skull or skeleton. Posada's skeleton pictures used satire: humour that criticises behaviour or power. Later artists helped make his image widely known. Its later link with Día de Muertos is one chapter in a longer history. Posada did not invent the older celebration. Together, the print and the museum ofrenda show how old practices, new art and changing audiences can keep a tradition alive.
read.sections.2.text.back:
An ofrenda gives memory a shape people can see. Photos, food, flowers and other objects can show who is being remembered. All of that also makes the room feel welcoming. The museum example in the photo is in Coyoacán, in Mexico City. That ofrenda has stepped levels, bright paper decorations and models of skeleton figures. Its file record says that ofrenda is dedicated to Mother Mary of Guadalupe. This display brings Catholic images and the activity of making festive decorations together in one public space. This display cannot represent every altar in people's homes.

Papel picado, that is, paper with cut-out designs, needs knowledge of pattern and material. Its makers cut designs into thin tissue paper and join the sheets into long strings. Skilled craftspeople can cut several layers at once, repeating a design. The paper may not last long, but the knowledge for making it continues. Preparing an altar that only stands for a short while also needs planning, choices and work. The photo of the finished result only shows part of all this.

Printed pictures have also changed how this celebration looks in public. José Guadalupe Posada's Calavera Catrina shows a skeleton wearing a luxurious hat. A calavera is a skull, or an artistic picture of a skull or skeleton. Posada's skeleton pictures used satire: humour that criticises behaviour or power. Artists who came later helped make his picture widely known. Its later connection with Día de Muertos is one chapter in a longer history. Posada did not create that older celebration. Together, the print and the museum ofrenda show how old practices, new art and changing audiences can keep a tradition alive.

sensitiveNotes.0.source: This lesson is about death and remembrance, and some learners may be grieving, including after losses linked to displacement. No one is asked to share about people they have lost, to describe a death, or to perform or take part in any practice. Don't ask for a bereavement example: the Write task uses only the photograph and the reading.
sensitiveNotes.0.back: This lesson is about death and remembering, and some learners may be grieving, including after losses connected with displacement. No one is asked to tell about people who have left them, to describe a death, or to perform or take part in any practice. sensitiveNotes.0.note: "people they have lost" is "orang yang telah meninggalkan mereka" (people who have left them), a gentle Indonesian way of saying it. "displacement" is "pengungsian", as Southeast Asia's TERMS.

sensitiveNotes.1.source: Describe beliefs as beliefs, and teach the communities as present-day makers and decision-makers. No learner is asked to share their religion. Avoid presenting the festival as an unchanged survival, a Mexican version of Halloween, or a tradition invented by Posada.
sensitiveNotes.1.back: Describe beliefs as beliefs, and teach those communities as makers and decision-makers of the present. No learner is asked to tell about their religion. Avoid presenting this celebration as a leftover of the past that has not changed, a Mexican version of Halloween, or a tradition created by Posada.

educatorNotes.1.source: Answer points for Write: a supported link between the arranged objects (paper, flowers, levels) and remembering, making or sharing meaning with an audience, recognising this as one public museum example. Accept continuity through learned skills, or change through new imagery. Don't infer a particular person being remembered from this Guadalupe-dedicated public display, and don't require a personal religious statement.
educatorNotes.1.back: Answer points for Write: a connection supported by evidence between the arranged objects (paper, flowers, levels) and remembering, making, or sharing meaning with an audience, while recognising that this is one example in a public museum. Accept continuity through learned skills, or change through new images. Don't conclude a particular person being remembered from this public display dedicated to Guadalupe, and don't require a personal religious statement.

educatorNotes.2.source: Source limits: Norma Cantú's family recollections are particular experiences, not universal rules. The Lam Museum's papel picado and Catrina pages support the paper-making and the print's later popularity; ignore the Catrina page's conflicting birth-year details and keep the Amon Carter's date and attribution. The Carter print is not the origin of the older festivities, and the photograph's record does not name the display's makers.
educatorNotes.2.back: Source limits: Norma Cantú's family memories are particular experiences, not rules that apply generally. The Lam Museum's papel picado and Catrina pages support the point about paper-making and the print's later fame; ignore the conflicting birth-year details on the Catrina page and keep the Amon Carter's date and attribution. The Carter's print is not the origin of the older celebrations, and the photo's record does not name the makers of its display.
educatorNotes.2.note: "Source limits" is "Batasan sumber", as Southeast Asia's TERMS ("limit" = batasan).
